title: The Sharpe Pint: SK Hynix's Mega Debut, the IRR Magic Trick, and Differentiable Markowitz

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a coffee, or if you're reading this on Sunday evening, maybe a pint. We've had a busy end to the trading week, with the AI hype machine finding a massive new gear, regulators playing party pooper in the commodities space, and the Fed doing its best impression of a deer in the headlights. Here is what you need to know to look smart in the office tomorrow.

sections.title: Daily Finance & Business News: Mega Debuts and Sunday Trading Bans

content.text: The AI hardware trade has just received its biggest validation yet, while commodity regulators have made it clear that some markets are simply too systemic to run 24/7.
SK Hynix’s Blockbuster $26.5bn Nasdaq Debut

South Korean memory giant SK Hynix made its highly anticipated Wall Street debut, raising a staggering $26.5 billion by pricing its American Depositary Shares (ADS) at $149 each. It is the largest foreign IPO in US history. The stock immediately popped, closing up 13.1% on its first day of trading.

items: Why it matters: SK Hynix is the undisputed king of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips, which are the secret sauce powering Nvidia and AMD’s AI processors. This massive debut proves that despite the growing chorus of bears warning about an 'AI capex bubble,' Wall Street’s appetite for the picks-and-shovels providers of the AI boom is still ravenous.

The City angle: This is a massive liquidity event and a huge win for the underwriting syndicate. For asset managers, it introduces a massive new liquid vehicle to play the AI hardware theme, which put immediate pressure on competitors like Micron (which slipped on the day).

Over a pint: 'SK Hynix raising $26.5bn on Nasdaq is a massive vote of confidence in the AI hardware layer. It shows that even if people are worried about software monetisation, the market is still more than happy to fund the physical infrastructure at eye-watering valuations.'

content.text: No Sunday Trading: CFTC Blocks CME’s 24/7 Oil Futures

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has stepped in to stay a self-certified contract from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) that would have launched 24/7 trading on crude oil futures starting Friday, July 10.

items: Why it matters: CME wanted to bring round-the-clock trading to crude oil, reflecting the global, continuous nature of energy markets (especially with the ongoing Middle East tensions). However, the CFTC is exercising its regulatory veto to assess the systemic risk, overnight liquidity, and clearing challenges of trading a major physical commodity 24/7.

The City angle: For quant desks and commodity traders, 24/7 trading would mean rewriting execution algorithms and staffing desks overnight. Regulators are deeply worried about 'flash crashes' in illiquid overnight hours when there are fewer market makers to absorb shocks.

Over a pint: 'The CFTC blocking CME's 24/7 oil trading plan shows regulators are terrified of overnight liquidity black holes. If you can trade crude at 3 AM on a Sunday, who is providing the backstop when geopolitical news breaks?'

content.text: Ceasefire Collapses, but Oil Keeps Its Cool

The weeks-long ceasefire between the US and Iran collapsed, leading to fresh military frictions and airstrikes. Despite the geopolitical flare-up, crude oil prices actually eased slightly on Friday, with Brent trading around $76.47 a barrel and WTI at $71.59.

items: Why it matters: While oil spiked to nearly $120 earlier in the conflict, the market seems to have priced in the geopolitical risk premium, or is betting that the Strait of Hormuz will remain open. It shows a fascinating decoupling of geopolitical headlines from immediate market panic.

The City angle: Macro funds and commodity traders are watching the Strait of Hormuz closely. The lack of a massive spike suggests that supply expectations are still relatively stable, or global demand concerns (especially from China/Europe) are offsetting the geopolitical risk.

Over a pint: 'It's wild how the market has shrugged off the US-Iran ceasefire collapse. Brent at $76 tells you that either the geopolitical risk premium is fully baked in, or macro traders are much more worried about global demand than supply disruptions.'

content.text: The Fed’s Semi-Annual Report: Clear as Mud

The Federal Reserve released its semi-annual Monetary Policy Report on Friday. It noted that inflation has risen this year and remains elevated, while the labor market remains stable. The FOMC has kept the federal funds rate at 3.5% to 3.75% since the beginning of the year.

items: Why it matters: This report sets the stage for Fed Chair Jerome Powell's upcoming congressional testimony. The Fed is in a tough spot: inflation is sticky and rising, but GDP growth is moderate and consumption is soft.
The City angle: Fixed income desks are parsing this for any hints on the next move. With rates held at 3.5%-3.75%, the Fed is trying to balance the dual mandate without triggering a hard landing.

Over a pint: 'The Fed's report confirms they are stuck in a holding pattern. Inflation is too sticky to cut, but soft consumer spending means they can't hike either. Powell's testimony next week is going to be a masterclass in saying nothing while looking deeply concerned.'

content.text: S&P 500 Earnings: Priced for Perfection (Again)

As the Q2 2026 earnings season begins, FactSet and LSEG reports show that consensus expects year-over-year earnings growth of 23.6% for the S&P 500. If realized, this will be the second consecutive quarter of growth above 20%. FactSet notes that with typical upside surprises, the final growth rate could top 29%.

items: Why it matters: The market is trading at a forward P/E of 20.5 (above the 5-year average of 19.9). To justify these valuations, companies must deliver on these massive earnings growth expectations. Micron has overtaken Nvidia as the largest contributor to Q2 earnings growth.
The City angle: For equity research and asset management, this earnings season is make-or-break. If companies miss these lofty targets, the tech-led rally could face a severe correction.

Over a pint: 'With the S&P 500 priced at 20.5x forward earnings, there's absolutely no room for error this earnings season. The market is expecting 23.6% growth, and if we don't get it, the valuation multiple is going to look very exposed.'

content.text: General Fusion SPACs Into the Public Eye

General Fusion completed its business combination with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III on July 10, 2026. It enters the public market with $150 million in cash and will begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker 'GFUZ' on July 13, 2026. It is the first publicly traded, pure-play fusion company.

items: Why it matters: Fusion energy has long been the '30 years away' technology, but the massive surge in electricity demand from AI data centers is driving a race to commercialize clean, baseload power. General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) technology is aiming for key technical milestones by 2028.

The City angle: This is a classic 'frontier tech' play. For ESG and venture-growth asset managers, it's a rare public vehicle to get exposure to fusion. However, SPACs have a terrible track record, and fusion is still highly speculative.

Over a pint: 'General Fusion listing as the first pure-play fusion stock is a fascinating thematic play. With AI data centers devouring power, the race for clean baseload energy is desperate. But let's be honest, investing in a SPAC-backed fusion company with a 2028 milestone target is the definition of high-beta.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: The Coiled Spring and London's Dealmaking Frenzy

content.text: The Coiled Spring: Megacaps Pin the Tape Ahead of CPI

Friday’s trading session was the financial equivalent of a coiled spring. On the surface, the headline indices looked like a slow summer afternoon: the S&P 500 ticked up 0.42% to 7,575.39, the Nasdaq added 0.29% to 26,281.61, and the Dow gained 0.29% to close at 52,637.01. But underneath, the overnight range was incredibly tight—the classic fingerprint of options dealers sitting 'long gamma' and pinning the index. When dealers are long gamma, they are forced to sell strength and buy weakness, effectively compressing the market into a tight band. They are holding the spring down, but they can only do it until a catalyst arrives. And next week is an absolute minefield of them, featuring June CPI (dropping Tuesday, 14 July), PPI, retail sales, and congressional testimony from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

The engine behind Friday's modest green close was, predictably, megacap tech. Meta ripped roughly 6% to cap its best week since early 2024, thanks to plans to bring 14 gigawatts of AI compute online by 2027 and the release of its Muse Spark 1.1 model. Nvidia also chipped in with a 4% gain. But the real star of the show was South Korean memory giant SK Hynix, which pulled off a blockbuster Nasdaq debut. Raising $26.5 billion by pricing its ADRs at $149, it popped 13.1% to close near $170, marking the largest foreign listing in US history. It's a massive validation of the AI hardware trade, but the underlying market breadth was terrible. The Russell 2000 fell 0.40% to 2,977.81, and the equal-weight S&P lagged. As any smart trader will tell you over a pint: narrow strength is not the same as market confirmation.
London's Dealmaking Frenzy and the OBR's Grim Reality Check

Over in London, the FTSE 100 managed a modest 0.24% gain on Friday to close at 10,497.29, though it still ended the week down 1.70% overall. The real action in the City wasn't macro; it was pure, unadulterated M&A. Vodafone jumped 12.6% after UAE's e& agreed to sell its 16.2% stake to French billionaire Xavier Niel's family investment vehicle for £4.4bn ($6bn), making him the largest shareholder. Meanwhile, in the FTSE 250, easyJet soared 14.5% after agreeing in principle to a £5.7bn ($7.65bn) takeover proposal from private equity giant Apollo, backing it over a rival approach from Castlelake. It seems the private equity vultures are still finding plenty of meat on the bones of UK plc.

But it wasn't all champagne in the City. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) dropped a fiscal bomb, warning that the UK's public finances are on an 'unsustainable' path. The watchdog calculated that the government will need spending cuts or tax rises of over £100 billion a year to stabilise debt. This is a brutal welcome gift for Andy Burnham, who is preparing to take over as Prime Minister later this month. If you're in UK rates or sterling, you'll want to watch how Burnham's team responds to this grim reality check—any sign of fiscal slippage could send Gilt yields marching higher.
Yen Repatriation Fears and the Geopolitical Oil Slide

In FX and commodities, the big story was the Japanese Yen. After hitting a painful 40-year low against the dollar earlier in the week, the Yen staged a sharp rally. Japan's Finance Minister Katayama sparked the move by suggesting the government wants to encourage domestic pension funds (think the colossal GPIF) to shift allocations away from foreign assets and back into domestic securities. If the world's largest pension fund starts repatriating cash, the USD/JPY unwind could get very messy, very quickly.

Meanwhile, the geopolitical premium in oil deflated slightly. Earlier in the week, a breakdown in the US-Iran ceasefire and fresh strikes sent Brent crude up 5% for the week. But on Friday, oil eased back (Brent to $76.50, WTI to $71.59) as Trump indicated technical-level talks would continue. Gold slipped to $4,115, and Bitcoin firmed above $64,000, while the VIX drifted down to 15.03, showing that for now, the market is happy to look past the Middle East and focus entirely on the upcoming inflation print.

sections.title: Financial Idea: The Subscription Line of Credit (and the IRR Magic Trick)

content.text: The Subscription Line of Credit (and the IRR Magic Trick)

If you have ever hung around a private equity fund's investor relations team, you will know they treat the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) like a sacred text. But behind some of those eye-watering 20%+ IRRs lies a clever piece of financial engineering that has nothing to do with fixing up businesses, and everything to do with a bank loan called a Subscription Line of Credit (SLC)—or simply, a 'sub line'.

Historically, when a PE fund wanted to buy a company, they would ring up their investors (the Limited Partners, or LPs) and say, 'Right, we need £50 million by next Friday.' This is a capital call. But calling capital takes time, creates administrative hassle, and—crucially—starts the clock on the IRR calculation the second the cash leaves the LP's bank account.

Enter the sub line. Instead of calling the LP's cash immediately, the PE fund takes out a short-term revolving loan from a bank, secured against the 'uncalled capital commitments' of those very same LPs. They use the bank's money to buy the company on Day 1, and only call the LP's cash to pay off the bank months—sometimes up to a year—later.
The Math of the Magic Trick
Because IRR is incredibly sensitive to when cash is drawn down, delaying the capital call works wonders for the spreadsheet. Let's look at a simple example:

items: Scenario A (No Sub Line): A fund calls £100m from LPs on Day 1. They hold the asset for 5 years and sell it for £200m. This is a 2.0x MoIC (Multiple on Invested Capital). The IRR is 14.9%.

Scenario B (With Sub Line): The fund buys the same asset on Day 1 using a sub line. They delay calling the LPs' cash until Year 1. The LPs only have their cash locked up for 4 years. When the asset is sold for £200m in Year 5, the MoIC is still 2.0x (ignoring minor interest costs for a second). But because the cash was only outstanding for 4 years, the IRR jumps to 18.9%.

content.text: By doing absolutely nothing to the underlying business, the GP (General Partner) has magically conjured an extra 4.0 percentage points of IRR.
Why It Matters (And Why LPs Are Fuming)

If the ultimate cash returned (the MoIC) is the same, why does this matter? Two words: Carried Interest. Most PE funds have a 'preferred return' or hurdle rate (typically 8% IRR). Once they cross that hurdle, the fund managers unlock their 20% performance fee (carry). By using sub lines to artificially inflate the IRR, a manager can smash through that 8% hurdle and pocket millions in carry, even if the actual, unlevered return of the investments was mediocre.

Furthermore, in today's higher interest rate environment, these sub lines are not cheap. If a fund is paying 6% or 7% interest to a bank just to delay a capital call, that interest expense drags down the actual cash returned to investors. The MoIC might drop from 2.0x to 1.95x. LPs are essentially paying bank fees to help GPs window-dress their own performance metrics.

This is why the Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) has stepped in with strict disclosure guidelines. They now push GPs to report performance both with and without the impact of subscription lines (levered vs. unlevered IRR).
Common Beginner Mistake

The classic rookie error is assuming that a higher IRR always means a better investment. IRR is a rate, not an absolute amount of wealth. If a fund returns a 50% IRR by doubling your money in six months (1.5x MoIC), that sounds amazing. But you then have to find somewhere else to reinvest that cash (reinvestment risk). Most institutional investors would gladly trade a high short-term IRR for a lower but steady 15% IRR that compounds their capital over a full decade (a 4.0x MoIC). You can't pay pensions with percentages; you pay them with pounds.
How to Use This in Interviews & Work Conversations

If you are interviewing for a role in private equity, private credit, or asset management, expect this to come up. A great way to show commercial maturity is to discuss the tension between IRR and MoIC.

items: The Interview Answer: 'While GPs love subscription lines because they compress the J-curve and boost IRR to hit hurdle rates, sophisticated LPs are increasingly focused on unlevered IRR and TVPI (Total Value to Paid-In capital). In a high-rate environment, the interest drag on sub lines can actually destroy cash-on-cash returns, making over-reliance on fund-level leverage a red flag.'

The Pub/Coffee Chat: 'Honestly, sub lines are the ultimate financial illusion. We are paying banks 7% interest just to delay a capital call by nine months so the GP can show a shiny 19% IRR instead of 15% and unlock their carry. It is like paying a premium to have your own money delivered to you later.'

content.text: The 'Predict-Then-Optimize' Trap

The standard workflow in quantitative portfolio management is a bit like buying a bespoke suit in two completely unrelated halves. First, you ask a machine learning model to guess your measurements (the return forecasting stage). Then, you hand those guesses to a Markowitz optimizer to construct the portfolio (the optimization stage). Unsurprisingly, the trousers end up around your ankles. This separation is known as the 'predict-then-optimize' paradigm, and it is fundamentally broken.

Why? Because standard regression models (like MSE) treat all prediction errors equally. They don't know—or care—whether a 1% error is on a high-beta stock that will dominate your portfolio, or a micro-cap you are legally barred from buying. The model wastes precious capacity trying to get the average error down across the entire universe, rather than focusing on the precision of the specific assets that actually matter to your specific investment mandate.
The Idea: End-to-End Decision-Focused Learning

To fix this, we need to smash the two stages together. Instead of training a model to minimize prediction error, we train it to directly maximize the downstream portfolio's realized utility (or Sharpe ratio), accounting for risk preferences, transaction costs, and real-world constraints. A new NBER working paper, 'Machine Learning Meets Markowitz' (February 2026), co-authored by Duke's Campbell Harvey (of Man Group and Research Affiliates fame) along with Yijie Wang, Hao Gao, Yan Liu, and Xinyuan Tao, takes this theory into the harsh light of real-world portfolio management.

By making the optimization step differentiable, the neural network can backpropagate through the Markowitz solver. If the model makes a prediction error that causes the optimizer to buy a toxic asset, the loss function penalises the model heavily. If it makes an error on an asset the portfolio doesn't even hold, the model barely cares. The model endogenously learns its own 'efficient frontier' tailored to the investor's exact constraints.
A Mini Technical Blueprint

Here is a simplified PyTorch illustration of how you construct a decision-focused loss function. Instead of calculating MSE, we compute the analytical portfolio weights from our predicted returns, calculate the realized utility, and backpropagate directly through the weights:

import torch

def end_to_end_loss(pred_returns, actual_returns, cov_matrix, risk_aversion=2.0):
    # Analytical mean-variance weights: w = (1/gamma) * inv(Sigma) * mu
    inv_cov = torch.inverse(cov_matrix)
    weights = (1.0 / risk_aversion) * torch.matmul(inv_cov, pred_returns)
    weights = torch.softmax(weights, dim=-1) # Ensure weights sum to 1
    
    # Realized utility calculation
    realized_return = torch.dot(weights, actual_returns)
    realized_variance = torch.dot(weights, torch.matmul(cov_matrix, weights))
    utility = realized_return - (risk_aversion / 2.0) * realized_variance
    
    return -utility
Why This Matters Over a Pint

items: The Interview Flex: If you are asked how to apply ML to asset allocation, do not say 'I'd predict returns with an LSTM and plug them into mean-variance.' That is incredibly outdated. Instead, explain that you would use decision-focused learning to backpropagate the portfolio's utility loss directly to the model parameters, ensuring the neural network prioritises accuracy where it actually impacts the weights.

The Parametric Portfolio Policy (PPP) Debate: You might hear quants argue that we should just use PPP (which maps signals directly to weights, bypassing return prediction entirely). But as Harvey and his co-authors point out, PPP fails for conservative, risk-averse investors because it lacks precise portfolio control and struggles to converge to the minimum-variance portfolio. The end-to-end framework bridges this gap by keeping the optimizer in the loop.

The 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' Risk: The massive caveat here is computational complexity and estimation error. Backpropagating through a quadratic program (QP) with hundreds of assets at every training epoch is incredibly heavy (though packages like cvxpylayers help). More importantly, if your covariance matrix is noisy, the end-to-end model will happily learn to exploit that noise, leading to spectacular out-of-sample disappointment.

sections.title: The Paper: Digital Safe Havens and the Economics of Tokenised Treasuries

content.text: Digital Safe Havens: The Economics of Tokenized Treasuries (NBER Working Paper 35412, July 2026) by Chen Lin, Eswar S. Prasad, Daniel Rabetti, and Che Zhang.

Why this one? Because tokenised real-world assets (RWAs)—specifically US Treasuries—have gone from a niche crypto experiment to a multi-billion-pound institutional playground. BlackRock's BUIDL fund has ballooned to nearly $2.85 billion, and Ondo's USDY is being passed around like a hot potato. But until now, we haven't had a proper, rigorous academic autopsy of how these things actually price, how they transmit monetary policy, and where the systemic plumbing might burst. This paper is that autopsy.
The Core Findings: Yield, Transmission, and Fragility

The authors look under the hood of these on-chain dollar instruments using a massive dataset of transactions, total value locked (TVL), and policy shocks. They break their findings down into three main pillars:

items: The Yield Anatomy: You can't just look at the headline yield. The authors decompose on-chain treasury yields into issuer fees, lending premia, leverage, basis-trade carry (think Ethena's USDe/USDtb), and 'collateral pledgability'. This last one is crucial: the ability to use these tokens as collateral in DeFi creates a massive 'implicit convenience yield' that traditional paper Treasuries simply can't match.

Heterogeneous Policy Transmission: When the Fed moves rates, how quickly does it hit the blockchain? It depends on the design. 'Administratively set' rates (like traditional tokenised money market funds) are slow and sticky. But 'basis-trade-backed' instruments (which rely on the futures-spot basis) react with massive, sometimes amplified, volatility to policy shocks.

The Safe Haven Paradox: During market panics, tokenised Treasuries act exactly like their off-chain cousins—capital floods into them as a digital safe haven. But this creates a new breed of systemic risk. The interaction between on-chain composability (tokens being looped and lent) and off-chain reserve structures (actual T-bills sitting in custody) creates weird, highly leveraged feedback loops, particularly on stablecoin balance sheets.

content.text: Key Quotes

...yields can be decomposed into distinct components reflecting issuer fees, lending premia, leverage, basis-trade carry, and collateral pledgability, with the latter generating economically large implicit convenience yields.

...tokenized Treasuries serve as digital safe havens during episodes of cross-asset stress... while simultaneously exposing new fragilities arising from the interaction between on-chain composability and off-chain reserve structures, particularly through stablecoin balance sheets.
What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skip the heavy econometric proofs and the methodology section where they build their affine pricing models (unless you're a quant portfolio manager looking to build an arbitrage bot). Instead, focus on Section 3 (the yield decomposition) and Section 5 (the safe haven and fragility analysis). That's where the real structural insights live.
How This Connects to You

If you're in asset management, you need to understand that tokenisation isn't just a cheaper way to settle trades; it changes the asset's economic properties by embedding a 'convenience yield' via DeFi utility. If you're in macro or markets, you need to realise that the on-chain dollar market is no longer isolated—it's a highly reactive, highly leveraged extension of the traditional financial system.
What to Say Over a Pint

items: Everyone talks about tokenisation as an operational efficiency play, but the real alpha is in the convenience yield. If you can pledge a tokenised T-bill as collateral in DeFi, you're unlocking a premium that traditional paper Treasuries simply can't match.

The plumbing is where it gets scary. When a risk-off event hits, the rush into tokenised Treasuries creates massive leverage loops on stablecoin balance sheets. We're essentially building a shadow banking system on public ledgers with zero central bank backstop.

content.text: Our Take

This paper is a must-read because it moves the tokenisation debate away from 'crypto-bro' hype and into hard, cold monetary economics. The reality is that as TradFi and DeFi merge, the boundaries of liquidity are blurring. Tokenised Treasuries are the bridge, but if the bridge is built on fragile stablecoin reserves and highly volatile basis trades, the next liquidity squeeze won't stay on-chain. It will spill right back into the real world. Read it before your next team meeting so you can sound like the smartest person in the room.

sections.title: People & Psychology: The Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect

content.text: The Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect

Picture this: you’re grabbing a flat white near Bank, scrolling through a major financial daily or a fresh sell-side research report. You spot an article covering your specific niche—say, UK mid-cap tech or structured credit. You read it and wince. The analyst has completely botched the facts, reversed cause and effect, and clearly doesn't know their bid from their ask. You laugh, shake your head at the state of broker research, and turn the page to an article about geopolitical tensions in East Asia or the future of solid-state batteries. Suddenly, your brain resets. You read every word of this new piece with rapt attention, absorbing it as absolute gospel. You have just fallen victim to the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect.

Coined by the novelist Michael Crichton (and cheekily named after his friend, the Nobel laureate physicist Murray Gell-Mann, to sound a bit more prestigious), the effect describes our bizarre tendency to spot glaring errors in a source’s coverage of our own field, yet completely trust that same source on topics we know nothing about. In ordinary life, if a mate consistently tells you absolute rubbish, you'd stop asking them for advice. In the City, however, we suffer from institutional amnesia. We treat generalist publications, broker research, and—increasingly in 2026—Large Language Models as infallible gurus the moment they pivot away from our immediate backyard.

Think about how this plays out in a typical investment committee. You might spend three days arguing over a 25-basis-point tweak to the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) in your DCF model because that’s the part you control. But when it comes to the long-term inflation rate or the terminal growth rate, you blindly plug in a 2.0% consensus figure sourced from a broad central bank forecast. You’ve spent 90% of your cognitive energy on the micro-details, while letting massive, unexamined macro assumptions slide in through the back door. Similarly, we often use LLMs for research. When we ask them about our specific domain, we spot their subtle hallucinations instantly. Yet, five minutes later, we ask the same model to summarise a complex regulatory framework in a foreign market and copy-paste the output directly into a client deck without a second thought.

items: Audit your inputs: If a broker report, news outlet, or AI tool is sloppy on the things you know intimately, assume they are just as sloppy on the things you don't. Treat generalist summaries as starting points, never as underwriting gospel.

Beware the 'One-Error' Pitch Killer: When pitching to clients or senior stakeholders, they will inevitably judge your entire presentation based on the one slide that covers *their* specific area of expertise. If you get a basic detail wrong about their sub-sector, they will assume the rest of your deck is equally flawed.

Challenge the 'sacrosanct' defaults: Don't fall into the trap of over-modelling the variables you understand while treating external consensus forecasts as absolute truth. If the Wall Street consensus is consistently wrong on interest rates, don't treat their forecasts as unshakeable pillars in your model.

content.text: "You read with exasperation or amusement the multiple errors in a story, and then turn the page... and read as if the rest of the newspaper was somehow more accurate... You turn the page, and forget what you know." — Michael Crichton
One line to remember: If they don't know your backyard, don't trust them to map the forest.
